solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Awfully idle pussies outside German city shops (13)

indicators.note: done awfully, the letters come out in a mess
the anagrammed letters sit outside the city

blocks.note: Essen, in the Ruhr, sits between the last two letters of the anagram

annotation.surface: Lazy cats lounging about outside the shops of a German city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pussies' is just cats, and 'outside' is not a place in the scene: the anagram wraps round the city, leaving a single S at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A plural noun for plural 'shops': these are shops selling prepared meats, cheeses and fine foods.

entries.clue: Announcement surprisingly neat and cordial (11)

indicators.note: the letters fall out in a surprising order

annotation.surface: Someone is pleasantly surprised by how tidy and friendly a public statement was.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' is not fodder: only NEAT and CORDIAL are rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a formal statement made public, as in a declaration of war.

entries.clue: Proposition from learner meeting novel woman (5)

blocks.note: Emma, heroine of Jane Austen's novel

annotation.surface: A learner driver chats up a woman in a novel way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel woman' reads as an unusual woman, but it is a woman from a novel: Austen's Emma. 'Proposition' is the mathematical sense, not a pass at someone.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical sense: in mathematics, a minor proposition proved as a stepping stone to a larger theorem.

entries.clue: NCO swallowing drug is not spiritual (9)

indicators.note: the NCO takes the drug inside him

blocks.note: a corporal is a non-commissioned officer
E = ecstasy; it goes in after the sixth letter

annotation.surface: A soldier caught taking drugs is judged to lack spirituality.
annotation.walkthrough: NCO stands for non-commissioned officer, a junior army rank; the surface's drug-taking soldier hides a simple swap of one rank word.
annotation.definitionFit: An antonym phrase: bodily and material, the opposite of spiritual.

entries.clue: Food and drink after this person’s restricted by disease (7)

indicators.note: the drink comes after the rest
the disease closes round I'M

blocks.note: this person is = I'M; it goes between T and B

annotation.surface: Someone complains that illness is keeping them from eating and drinking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This person' is the setter speaking of themself, so 'this person's' is I'M.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: a specific dish of meat or fish baked in a drum-shaped mould.

entries.clue: Report of wickedness unusual in church body (5)

indicators.note: a report is what is heard, so the letters come by sound

annotation.surface: News of unusual wickedness inside a church's governing council.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as a container instruction but is only a link joining the wordplay to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the governing assembly of clergy and officials in a church.

entries.clue: Signing up for Lent, men denied minimum of food sadly (9)

indicators.note: the first word is refused a letter
the least of 'food' is its first letter
the letters end up in a sorry state

blocks.note: taken as written, before it loses a letter
first letter of Food, the letter denied to FOR, leaving OR

annotation.surface: Men who give up food for Lent are unhappy about having signed up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like a link word, but it is fodder: it loses the F of 'food' before the letters are mixed.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun phrase matching a noun: the act of putting your name on a register.

entries.clue: Jock getting caught out as one having too much whisky? (3)

indicators.note: Jock gets the treatment that follows
the C for caught is taken out

blocks.note: Jock is a nickname for a Scotsman
c = caught, the cricket scoring abbreviation; removed

annotation.surface: A Scotsman thrown out for drinking too much whisky.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jock' is a British slang name for a Scot. The question mark flags that a sot can drink too much of anything, not just whisky.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a habitual drunkard, pictured here with the Scot's national drink.

entries.clue: Yell, not about deception (4)

indicators.note: the letters for 'about' are not there

blocks.note: re = about; these two letters are removed

annotation.surface: Someone insists they are not shouting about being cheated.
annotation.walkthrough: RE for 'about' comes from the Latin in memo headings.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a dishonest trick to cheat someone.

entries.clue: A Parisian charging engineers to assess pay (10)

indicators.note: the French article charges into the engineers

blocks.note: REME = Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers
a in French; it goes in before REME's last letter

annotation.surface: A Frenchman billing some engineers for a pay review.
annotation.walkthrough: REME is the British Army's engineering corps. 'Pay' looks like a noun in the surface but works as a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to pay someone for work or services.

entries.clue: Dad rushed round, one with a sort of obsession (8)

annotation.surface: A father dashing about, gripped by a fixation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round' is not a reversal or container instruction; it is simply O.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose category: an irrational, fixed suspicion of others is a kind of obsession.

entries.clue: Trick lord falling into river (6)

indicators.note: the lord drops inside the river

blocks.note: the Dee, a river in Wales, England and Scotland
lud, as in 'm'lud' in court; it drops into the river

annotation.surface: A prank in which a nobleman topples into a river.
annotation.walkthrough: LUD is the old form of 'lord' kept alive in the courtroom address 'm'lud'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to mislead someone into a false belief.

entries.clue: Record author finally prepared for publication is no longer valid (11)

indicators.note: only the final letter of 'author' is taken

annotation.surface: An author's account, once edited for the press, no longer holds up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Record' looks like a verb or a document in the surface, but it is a vinyl disc.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective for an adjective phrase: a claim shown to be false no longer stands.

entries.clue: Female boss, a long time with little right, in muddle (10)

indicators.note: the pieces go in the muddle

blocks.note: R is the short form of right
a mess is a muddle; it wraps round the other pieces after its first letter

annotation.surface: A female boss who has been in a muddle for ages.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A long time' is AN AGE, not A plus a separate word for time.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a woman in charge of a shop, restaurant or office.

entries.clue: Deals with a daughter needing wardrobe items (9)

blocks.note: d = daughter, as in family trees

annotation.surface: A parent sorting out a daughter's need for new clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Needing' joins the pieces; the definition is a verb phrase, so the answer is a verb too.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to tackle a problem or issue.

entries.clue: Gets on horses, not entirely secure at first (9)

indicators.note: SURE loses its last letter
the shortened word comes first

annotation.surface: A rider climbs onto horses, unsteady at first.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gets on' is both the definition and part of the horse picture.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal verb sense: to climb up onto or get on top of something.

entries.clue: Get rid of heartless language (4)

indicators.note: the middle letter is removed

blocks.note: erase = get rid of; its middle letter A goes

annotation.surface: A call to abolish a cruel way of speaking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heartless language' reads as unkind speech, but 'heartless' works on the phrase before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: an old name for the Gaelic of Scotland or Ireland.

entries.clue: Unconventional pronouncement of writer (4)

indicators.note: a pronouncement is spoken, so the name is taken by sound

annotation.surface: An eccentric remark made by an author.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface nods at Wilde himself, famous for unconventional pronouncements.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: out of the ordinary, unrestrained by convention.

entries.clue: New retrial with boy likely to result in freedom (10)

indicators.note: the letters are made new, into a fresh arrangement

annotation.surface: A young defendant's fresh trial might set him free.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a long adjective phrase; the surface makes it sound like a verdict forecast.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective phrase glossing an adjective: tending to set people free.

entries.clue: English inventor of container carried by infant (7)

indicators.note: the infant holds the container inside

blocks.note: a bag is a container; it goes before the infant's last letter

annotation.surface: A baby clutching a box made by an English inventor.
annotation.walkthrough: Charles Babbage designed the mechanical computers called the Difference and Analytical Engines.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Victorian mathematician whose calculating engines foreshadowed computers.

entries.clue: Consume with lack of seriousness, we hear (6)

indicators.note: what we hear is the sound, not the spelling

annotation.surface: Eating something as a joke, so it is said.
annotation.walkthrough: The G is soft, so the answer and the phrase for joking sound the same.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to take food or drink into the body.

entries.clue: Small bird atop an enormously important person (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, TIT sits above AN

blocks.note: a tit is a small songbird

annotation.surface: A little bird perched on the head of a VIP.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Enormously' is part of the definition, not an instruction: the giants of Greek myth give the word its size.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: after the giant gods of Greek myth, a person of towering power.

entries.clue: Security device gets ordered outside — it stops invasions (8)

indicators.note: the word for 'ordered' goes outside the device

blocks.note: a lock; it goes after BADE's first letter

annotation.surface: A lock is fitted outside to keep intruders out.
annotation.walkthrough: BADE is the old past tense of 'bid', as in 'she bade him leave'.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a sealing-off of ports or borders stops anything getting through.

entries.clue: Foreign character ending in dark, only half manifest (5)

indicators.note: take the final letter of 'dark'
just the first half of the word is used

annotation.surface: A shadowy foreigner whose presence is only half visible.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Foreign character' means a letter of another alphabet, here Greek.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: the tenth letter of the Greek alphabet.

entries.clue: Show where to go and use hot running water (5-5)

indicators.note: the letters run about into a new order

blocks.note: rain is water from the sky

annotation.surface: Instructions for directions and a hot shower.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Running water' is a natural phrase, but 'running' acts on 'use hot' and 'water' stands alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A euphemism: teaching a pet where to relieve itself is showing it where to go.

entries.clue: Gosh, male offers some resistance! (3)

annotation.surface: A man surprised to meet a little opposition.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Resistance' is electrical, not opposition, so the definition asks for a measured amount of it.
annotation.definitionFit: A unit for its quantity: this is the SI unit of electrical resistance, so one is some resistance.

entries.clue: Stone, hard, in bit of fruit? (4)

blocks.note: a pit is a fruit stone

annotation.surface: A hard stone found inside a piece of fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link, not a container instruction; the question mark admits the answer is only one bit of a fruit.
annotation.definitionFit: A part for the whole's part: the white spongy layer under citrus peel.

entries.clue: Fail to get support after maiden and I separate (13)

indicators.note: the support comes after the other pieces

blocks.note: m = maiden, a maiden over in cricket scoring

annotation.surface: A failed attempt to win backing after a young woman and the speaker split up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maiden' is M from cricket scorecards, where a maiden is an over with no runs. 'Get' means understand, not obtain.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to 'get' something is to grasp it, so failing to get is grasping it wrongly.
